subtopic_detail: Choosing decompression over conservative therapy in median neuropathy with motor signs
stem:
You are the general medical registrar reviewing a 52 year old cleaner in the ambulatory clinic. For nine months she has been waking two or three times a night with both hands feeling dead, and she now says the numbness in her right hand never fully goes away and she keeps dropping her keys.

Neck rotation and extension are full and pain free, and the triceps and biceps reflexes are symmetrical. On the right there is visible flattening of the muscle bulk at the base of the thumb and thumb abduction against resistance is weak. Sensation is reduced over the pulps of the right thumb, index and middle fingers but preserved over the skin of the thenar eminence itself.

data_table.Examination: Right abductor pollicis brevis power 3 out of 5, left grip and thumb abduction normal, no wasting of the first dorsal interosseous
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function within normal limits, fasting glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine
options.rationale: A C6 radiculopathy is the near pair but would give neck pain on movement, an altered biceps reflex and sensory change extending onto the forearm, none of which is present (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Carpal tunnel syndrome).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Carpal tunnel syndrome

options.text: Trial a nocturnal wrist splint held in neutral for six weeks
options.rationale: Night splinting is the first line only for intermittent symptoms without motor signs, and offering it here delays release while the thenar muscle continues to denervate (Source: RACGP: Carpal tunnel syndrome in general practice).
source_refs: RACGP: Carpal tunnel syndrome in general practice

options.text: Inject corticosteroid into the carpal tunnel under ultrasound
options.rationale: Injection gives useful but usually temporary relief in mild to moderate disease and is a reasonable bridge in pregnancy, whereas established wasting is an indication to proceed to definitive release (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Carpal tunnel syndrome).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Carpal tunnel syndrome

options.text: Refer for surgical decompression of the carpal tunnel
options.rationale: Persistent sensory loss with wasting and weakness of abductor pollicis brevis defines severe disease, and once axonal motor loss is established conservative measures rarely reverse it, so surgical release is the intervention that preserves function (Source: RACGP: Carpal tunnel syndrome in general practice).
source_refs: RACGP: Carpal tunnel syndrome in general practice

options.text: Prescribe a two week tapering course of oral prednisolone
options.rationale: Oral corticosteroid produces only short lived benefit measured in weeks and carries systemic risk without altering the compressive mechanism (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

explanation.summary: Median nerve compression at the wrist is graded clinically by whether symptoms are intermittent, constant, or accompanied by motor loss, and that grading drives the management branch rather than the duration of symptoms alone. Sparing of sensation over the thenar eminence is the anatomical clue that the lesion sits under the flexor retinaculum, because the palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve proximal to the tunnel. Secondary causes worth excluding before surgery include hypothyroidism, diabetes, pregnancy, acromegaly and inflammatory arthritis. Nerve conduction studies grade severity and are usually requested by the operating surgeon, but a clear clinical picture with wasting does not need them to justify referral. Delay matters because thenar recovery after release is far less complete once wasting is visible.
key_points: Constant numbness plus abductor pollicis brevis weakness or wasting marks severe disease and warrants surgical referral.
Preserved sensation over the thenar eminence localises the lesion to within the tunnel rather than proximally.
Night splinting and corticosteroid injection are for intermittent symptoms without motor signs.
Full pain free neck movement with symmetrical reflexes argues against a C6 radiculopathy.
Check thyroid function and glucose, since correctable causes change the conservative options.
explanation.pearls: Thenar wasting means the axons are already dying: functional recovery of abductor pollicis brevis after release falls sharply once wasting is visible, which is why severe disease is referred rather than splinted for six weeks.

sources.label: RACGP: Carpal tunnel syndrome in general practice
BMJ Best Practice: Carpal tunnel syndrome

subtopic_detail: Imaging choice in inflammatory back pain when plain radiographs of the sacroiliac joints are normal
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 26 year old carpenter referred with fourteen months of low back pain. He tells you the pain wakes him in the early hours and that he has to get up and walk about, and that he feels loosest after a shift rather than after a rest day. Stiffness on waking lasts about an hour.

He had a painful red right eye treated with steroid drops last year. Lumbar flexion is reduced with a modified Schober of 3.5 cm and chest expansion is 4 cm. Plain radiographs of the sacroiliac joints reported today are normal, and straight leg raise is negative bilaterally with normal ankle and knee reflexes.

data_table.Examination: Modified Schober 3.5 cm, chest expansion 4 cm, sacroiliac joints tender to direct pressure
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 14 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 32 mm/h (1-20), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Computed tomography of the sacroiliac joints without intravenous contrast
options.rationale: Computed tomography shows established erosion and ankylosis better than plain film but cannot show marrow oedema, so it misses the early inflammatory phase while delivering pelvic radiation to a young man (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis).

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints with fluid sensitive sequences
options.rationale: Structural change on plain film lags the onset of inflammation by years, so a normal radiograph does not exclude the diagnosis and marrow oedema in the subchondral bone on a fluid sensitive sequence is what establishes non radiographic disease (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis).

options.text: Human leucocyte antigen B27 typing on a peripheral venous blood sample
options.rationale: The allele is carried by roughly 8 per cent of the Australian population so a positive result raises but does not confirm probability, and it is used to weight the classification criteria rather than to replace imaging (Source: ASAS classification criteria for axial spondyloarthritis).
source_refs: ASAS classification criteria for axial spondyloarthritis

options.text: Repeat plain radiographs of the sacroiliac joints in twelve months
options.rationale: Waiting a year to see whether erosions appear concedes an untreated inflammatory year, which is the specific anti pattern that the non radiographic category was created to prevent (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis).

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine with gadolinium contrast
options.rationale: Lumbar imaging targets disc and nerve root disease, which the negative straight leg raise and normal reflexes already argue against, and gadolinium adds nothing when fluid sensitive sequences answer the question (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

explanation.summary: Inflammatory back pain is defined by onset before age 45, insidious onset, improvement with exercise but not rest, night pain with waking, and duration beyond three months. Recognising it matters because the mechanical pattern is vastly more common and gets managed with reassurance and activity, whereas the inflammatory pattern needs a rheumatologist, a scheduled non steroidal anti inflammatory trial and consideration of biologic therapy. Acute anterior uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease are the extra articular partners that raise pre test probability substantially. The radiographic and non radiographic forms sit on one disease spectrum and respond similarly to treatment, so the absence of erosions is not a reason to withhold referral. Untreated axial inflammation over years produces syndesmophytes and irreversible loss of spinal mobility.
key_points: Normal sacroiliac radiographs do not exclude axial spondyloarthritis; structural change lags inflammation by years.
Fluid sensitive magnetic resonance sequences show subchondral marrow oedema, the finding that defines non radiographic disease.
Improvement with exercise and not with rest, plus night waking, is the inflammatory pattern.
Acute anterior uveitis is the commonest extra articular feature and should prompt the question in a young person with back pain.
Human leucocyte antigen B27 weights probability but is neither necessary nor sufficient for diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: Scheduled rather than as needed non steroidal anti inflammatory therapy for at least two to four weeks at maximum tolerated dose is the recognised first line, and failure of two such agents is the usual gateway to a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor.

sources.label: ASAS classification criteria for axial spondyloarthritis

subtopic_detail: Selecting the first agent to withdraw after recurrent falls in a resident on multiple medicines
stem:
You are the visiting medical officer at a residential aged care facility reviewing an 84 year old woman after her third fall in ten weeks. Staff say she is unsteady when she gets up to the toilet before dawn and that she seems foggy until mid morning.

She has been taking nitrazepam 10 mg at night for three years, started for insomnia during a hospital admission. Lying and standing blood pressures are 138/78 mmHg and 134/76 mmHg. Her gait is wide based and slow but she has no tremor, no cogwheeling and normal ankle jerks, and the timed up and go is 21 seconds. Vitamin B12, calcium and thyroid function are within normal limits, and she has been on cholecalciferol for two years.

data_table.Medications: Nitrazepam 10 mg nocte, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nocte, sertraline 50 mg daily, pantoprazole 20 mg daily, cholecalciferol 1000 units daily
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 58 mL/min/1.73m2, sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), haemoglobin 126 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: Which medication change would you make first?

options.text: Halve the perindopril dose and review the blood pressure in a fortnight
options.rationale: Antihypertensives are a legitimate falls target but the paired lying and standing readings show a drop of only 4 mmHg, which removes postural hypotension as the mechanism here (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people).
source_refs: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people

options.text: Cease the atorvastatin given her age and limited life expectancy
options.rationale: Statin withdrawal is a reasonable later conversation about benefit horizon but statins do not cause unsteadiness or morning sedation, so it does not address the fall mechanism (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people).
source_refs: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people

options.text: Taper and cease the nitrazepam over eight to twelve weeks
options.rationale: A long acting benzodiazepine accumulates in an older person with reduced renal clearance and produces exactly this pattern of pre dawn unsteadiness with morning cognitive slowing, and gradual withdrawal reduces fall rates without precipitating a withdrawal syndrome (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Cease the sertraline because of the fall risk in older women
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants do raise fall and hyponatraemia risk, but her sodium is normal and abrupt withdrawal risks relapse of depression, so it ranks behind the sedative with the longer half life (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Cease the pantoprazole and review reflux symptoms after four weeks
options.rationale: Long term proton pump inhibitor use is worth reviewing for fracture and infection risk, but it does not cause gait instability and stopping it will not change tonight's fall risk (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people).
source_refs: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people

explanation.summary: Falls in residential care are almost always multifactorial, and a structured review separates the modifiable contributors into medicines, vision, footwear, environment, continence and gait. Among medicines, the sedative hypnotics, antipsychotics and anticholinergics carry the strongest and most reversible association, and long acting agents matter more than short acting ones because the drug is still present at the pre dawn toilet trip. Deprescribing is done one agent at a time so that the effect of each withdrawal is interpretable, starting with the drug that has the weakest indication and the strongest harm signal. Abrupt cessation of a benzodiazepine taken for years risks rebound insomnia, agitation and seizures, so the withdrawal is staged over weeks with the resident and family informed. A timed up and go above 12 seconds already flags a person who needs a physiotherapy strength and balance program alongside the medication change.
key_points: Long acting benzodiazepines are the highest yield first deprescribing target after falls in aged care.
Paired lying and standing pressures with a small drop remove postural hypotension from the differential.
Withdraw one agent at a time so the effect of each change can be judged.
Taper rather than stop, because seizures and rebound insomnia follow abrupt withdrawal after chronic use.
Pair the medication change with a strength and balance program and a vitamin D review.
explanation.pearls: Nitrazepam has an elimination half life of about 24 to 30 hours and is longer still in an older person with reduced clearance, which is why the 10 pm dose is still acting at the 5 am toilet trip that produced the fall.

sources.label: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people

subtopic_detail: Recognising a delayed multiorgan drug hypersensitivity and committing to systemic corticosteroid
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 58 year old man with five days of fever and a spreading itchy red rash that began on his trunk. His wife says his face has puffed up so much that he looks like a different man.

He started allopurinol thirty four days ago after two attacks of gout and takes nothing else new. The rash is a confluent morbilliform eruption over more than 60 per cent of his body surface with marked facial oedema. There are no target lesions, no mucosal erosions and Nikolsky sign is negative. He has tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 1.9 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), white cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), alanine aminotransferase 340 U/L (less than 41), creatinine 142 micromol/L (60-110), blood cultures collected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue allopurinol and add oral cetirizine with topical betamethasone
options.rationale: Continuing the culprit drug in a reaction with hepatic and renal involvement allows the syndrome to escalate, and antihistamines relieve itch without touching the underlying T cell driven organ injury (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Cease allopurinol and observe on supportive care without systemic therapy
options.rationale: Withdrawal alone suffices for a simple morbilliform exanthem but not once transaminases and creatinine are rising, because the reaction characteristically continues to worsen for weeks after the drug is stopped (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Cease allopurinol and commence oral prednisolone 1 mg per kg daily
options.rationale: Fever with facial oedema, eosinophilia above 1.5 x10^9/L, lymphadenopathy and hepatitis appearing three to eight weeks after drug exposure is the recognised pattern, and systemic corticosteroid with a slow taper over six to eight weeks is the accepted treatment for visceral involvement (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Cease allopurinol and commence intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kg
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin is used in epidermal necrolysis where keratinocyte apoptosis and skin detachment dominate, and the negative Nikolsky sign with intact mucosae places this on a different axis from that diagnosis (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms

options.text: Commence intravenous flucloxacillin and await the blood culture result
options.rationale: A febrile rash with lymphadenopathy invites an infective label, but eosinophilia with transaminitis points away from staphylococcal infection and a new beta lactam risks adding a second sensitising drug (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Delayed multiorgan drug hypersensitivity is distinguished from a simple exanthem by its long latency, its systemic features and the fact that it keeps evolving after the drug is withdrawn. Allopurinol, the aromatic anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, vancomycin and minocycline account for most Australian cases. Liver involvement is the commonest visceral manifestation and the usual cause of death, while thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes can appear months into recovery, so follow up thyroid function and glucose are scheduled rather than optional. Reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 is characteristic and partly explains the relapsing course during steroid taper. The culprit drug and its cross reactors must be recorded as an adverse drug reaction, since rechallenge produces a faster and more severe episode.
key_points: Latency of two to eight weeks distinguishes this reaction from an immediate hypersensitivity or a simple exanthem.
Eosinophilia, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy and transaminitis together make the diagnosis.
Negative Nikolsky sign with intact mucosae argues against epidermal necrolysis.
Systemic corticosteroid with a taper over six to eight weeks is indicated once visceral organs are involved.
Schedule thyroid function and glucose testing for months after recovery.
explanation.pearls: Taper prednisolone over at least six to eight weeks rather than two, because rapid withdrawal reliably produces a rebound flare of rash and hepatitis driven by herpesvirus reactivation.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms

subtopic_detail: Interpreting a modestly raised prolactin alongside a large pituitary mass
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar seeing a 34 year old woman referred with fifteen months of absent periods and milky discharge from both breasts. She has not been pregnant, has never breastfed, and takes no antipsychotic, antiemetic or antidepressant medication.

Confrontation testing shows loss of the outer half of each visual field. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary reports a 3.4 cm sellar mass with suprasellar extension compressing the optic chiasm. Her serum prolactin, taken as a single unstressed sample, is 1750 mIU/L. Thyroid function and morning cortisol are within normal limits and her renal function is normal.

data_table.Examination: Bitemporal field loss on confrontation, no acral enlargement, no proximal weakness, no striae
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 1750 mIU/L (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, creatinine within normal limits, beta human chorionic gonadotrophin not detected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for urgent transsphenoidal decompression of the sellar mass
options.rationale: Surgery is the right answer for a chiasmal compressing mass that is not prolactin secreting, but committing to theatre before the prolactin is correctly measured risks operating on a tumour that would shrink on a tablet (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Commence cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly and repeat imaging at three months
options.rationale: Starting a dopamine agonist on an uncorrected result gambles that the mass is lactotroph derived, and a non secreting adenoma treated this way loses months of vision while the chiasm stays compressed (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Request measurement of macroprolactin on the stored serum sample
options.rationale: Macroprolactin is the mirror image problem, an inert immunoglobulin bound complex that makes prolactin look falsely high in an asymptomatic person, so it explains an unexpectedly raised result rather than an unexpectedly low one (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Hyperprolactinaemia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Hyperprolactinaemia

options.text: Measure insulin like growth factor 1 and an overnight dexamethasone suppression test
options.rationale: Screening for co secretion of growth hormone or cortisol is reasonable in a large adenoma but neither acromegalic features nor cushingoid features are present, and it does not resolve the discrepancy driving the treatment decision (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Request repeat prolactin measurement performed on serially diluted serum
options.rationale: A 3.4 cm lactotroph tumour should generate a prolactin in the tens of thousands, and when antibody binding sites are saturated the assay reports a falsely low value, so dilution unmasks the true concentration and decides between a tablet and an operation (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Hyperprolactinaemia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Hyperprolactinaemia

explanation.summary: Prolactin concentration scales with lactotroph tumour volume, so the size of the mass and the height of the hormone should match, and a mismatch is itself the diagnostic finding. A large mass with only a modest elevation has two explanations: a non secreting lesion raising prolactin by compressing the stalk and interrupting dopamine delivery, or a genuine macroprolactinoma whose result is artefactually low because the immunoassay is saturated. Stalk effect rarely pushes prolactin above about 2000 to 3000 mIU/L, so the ceiling is the clue. The distinction is decisive because a true macroprolactinoma is treated medically with a dopamine agonist that usually shrinks the tumour and restores vision, whereas a non secreting adenoma compressing the chiasm goes to surgery. Any drug history of antipsychotics, metoclopramide, domperidone or high dose oestrogen, plus pregnancy, hypothyroidism and renal failure, must be excluded before the tumour is blamed.
key_points: Prolactin should be proportional to lactotroph tumour size; a mismatch demands explanation before treatment.
Assay saturation causes a falsely low result with very large tumours and is unmasked by serial dilution.
Macroprolactin causes the opposite artefact, a falsely high result in an asymptomatic person.
Stalk compression alone rarely raises prolactin beyond about 2000 to 3000 mIU/L.
A confirmed macroprolactinoma is treated with a dopamine agonist first, not with surgery, even with chiasmal compression.
explanation.pearls: Ask the laboratory specifically for a 1 in 100 dilution when a pituitary mass larger than 3 cm returns a prolactin under about 4000 mIU/L; the undiluted assay can under report a true value of more than 100000 mIU/L.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Hyperprolactinaemia
